name: Block Structure
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: What's Actually Inside a Block
lesson.summary: A block is a data container with two main parts, a header holding metadata and the previous block's hash, and a body holding the list of transactions, and understanding this structure is key to understanding how a blockchain actually stores information.
lesson.body:
The previous section defined a blockchain as a chain of blocks, but treated a "block" as a black box, essentially a card with a fingerprint on it. It is time to open that box. A block is, at its core, a data structure with two distinct parts: a header, which is a relatively small section of metadata about the block, and a body, which holds the actual payload, typically a list of transactions. This split matters enormously for how efficiently a blockchain can be verified, which a later section on block headers explores in more depth.

The body is the part most people picture when they think of a block: an ordered list of transactions that occurred during that block's time window. On Bitcoin, that means transfers of bitcoin between addresses. On Ethereum, it can also include calls to smart contracts. The body is typically the largest part of a block by far, since a single block can bundle anywhere from a few to several thousand transactions depending on the network and how full the transactions are.

The header is smaller but arguably more important structurally, because it is what makes the block fit into the blockchain definition from the previous section. It contains the cryptographic hash of the previous block's header, a timestamp, and, depending on the network's consensus mechanism, additional fields used to validate the block, such as a proof of work nonce or other consensus related data. The header also typically contains a single hash summarizing the entire body, often built as a Merkle tree, so that verifying the body's integrity does not require re-hashing every individual transaction by hand each time.

This two-part structure exists for a practical reason: not every participant in a blockchain network needs or wants to store and check every transaction ever made. A device with limited storage can download just the sequence of block headers, which is dramatically smaller than the full chain, verify that the headers link together correctly and were produced according to the network's rules, and trust the accumulated work embedded in that header chain, without ever downloading the full transaction bodies. This distinction between checking headers and checking full bodies becomes central later in this course when comparing full nodes to lighter weight participants.

A concrete sense of scale: a Bitcoin block header is a fixed 80 bytes, regardless of whether the block it belongs to contains one transaction or four thousand. The body, by contrast, can run to over a million bytes when full. That asymmetry, a tiny fixed size header standing in for a much larger variable size body, is what makes it possible for the block structure to scale to a global network without every participant needing supercomputer level storage and bandwidth just to keep up.
